cf.title: Use C11 alignas instead of palloc/malloc for alignment

input.subject: Use C11 alignas instead of palloc/malloc for alignment

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and none is fatal. Three fixable points remain. standards-compat-2 asks whether the rename in 0001 is worth a compile break for the out-of-tree users in message #8. standards-compat-1 shows that 0003 reuses the old name with 8-byte alignment. maintenance-fit-1 notes that the per-record memset in 0005 has no timing.

brief.title: Use C11 alignas instead of palloc/malloc for aligned buffers
brief.problem: Several places call palloc() or malloc() only to get an aligned buffer, which the author finds more complex than needed. The thread names no user-facing problem; this is internal refactoring. Later versions also target static variables in XLogRecordAssemble(), which get in the way of multi-threading.
brief.proposed_design: The patch replaces those allocations with local variables declared with alignas(MAXIMUM_ALIGNOF) or with existing AlignedBlock types. It renames PGAlignedXLogBlock to PGIOAlignedXLogBlock, and an optional XXX patch reintroduces PGAlignedXLogBlock as a MAXALIGNed type. It also adds an assertion for HEADER_SCRATCH_SIZE and moves the XLogRecordAssemble() workspace into a zeroed local in XLogInsert().
user_visible_surface: C API: type PGAlignedXLogBlock renamed to PGIOAlignedXLogBlock in c.h; extensions using the old name fail to compile.
C API: optional patch 0003 reintroduces PGAlignedXLogBlock with MAXALIGN instead of PG_IO_ALIGN_SIZE alignment.
C API: XLogReader struct definition in xlogreader.h changes.
author_claims: Using alignas with local variables is much simpler than palloc/malloc for aligned buffers.
Previous alignment guarantees are kept; MAXIMUM_ALIGNOF and max_align_t should be the same in practice.
The copy_file() and InitWalRecovery() allocations stay dynamic, for buffer size and storage reasons.
Reusing the name PGAlignedXLogBlock for a different alignment without a gap between releases is risky, so 0003 is marked XXX.
brief.thread_state: Heikki, Andres and Andrew commented; the author addressed them in v3/v4, and the pgindent fix was committed separately. Manuel tested both 0003 options and the WAL padding, Rui found no issues, and Linden suggested static const zero buffers; whether to apply 0003 and Linden's suggestion are still open.
unclear: The author has not decided between shipping 0001 alone or also 0003.
The author has not replied to Linden's suggestion to make the zero buffers in _mdfd_getseg() and dsm_impl_mmap() static const.
The thread does not say whether moving a 952-byte workspace onto the XLogInsert() stack has any measured performance cost.
The material does not list all converted call sites or the stack size each one adds.

objections.title: Renaming PGAlignedXLogBlock breaks known extensions for naming consistency only
objections.failure_scenario: Maintainers of pg_tde, pg_flashback, WAL-DIFF and similar tools build against the next major release. Compilation fails on PGAlignedXLogBlock, and they must add version-conditional code although nothing in their behaviour changes.
objections.argument: Message #8 lists at least seven out-of-tree projects that use the type for plain WAL page buffers. Patch 0001 gives them no functional gain; its stated reason is symmetry with PGAlignedBlock and PGIOAlignedBlock. A compatibility alias would keep them building, but it would also block the later MAXALIGNed reuse of the name. The proposal does not weigh these options. A committer would likely ask whether the naming symmetry is worth a break that the project chooses on purpose.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a rename without a compatibility alias better for the projects in message #8 than keeping the old name and adding a separate name for a MAXALIGNed block?

critic.reasoning: Compile breaks with a named replacement are normal across major versions, so the cost is small. But the series does not need 0001, and the thread does not weigh keeping the old name and choosing a new name for a MAXALIGNed block.

objections.title: Patch 0003 reuses an existing type name with weaker alignment
objections.failure_scenario: An extension declares PGAlignedXLogBlock and reads WAL with O_DIRECT. After upgrade it still compiles, but the buffer is only 8-byte aligned. pread fails with EINVAL on ext4 and works on btrfs, so the failure shows up only on some customer systems.
objections.argument: Message #8 measured this: with 0001-0005, alignof(PGAlignedXLogBlock) drops from 4096 to 8, and an O_DIRECT read fails on ext4 but succeeds on btrfs. Message #7 already doubts reusing the name without a gap, and 0003 is still marked XXX. The same type name gives a different contract with no compile-time signal. Manuel found no direct-I/O user, but a GitHub search on default branches is only a lower bound.
objections.author_must_show: If 0003 goes in, how many releases will separate the rename from the reintroduced name, and what tells a direct-I/O user that the alignment changed?

critic.reasoning: Message #8 measured the case: with 0003 the old name compiles, and an O_DIRECT read fails with EINVAL on ext4. Message #7 shares the doubt, but v4 still carries 0003 and states no gap, so the question is open.

objections.title: XLogInsert() now zeroes a 952-byte workspace on every WAL record
objections.failure_scenario: Every backend that writes WAL now zeroes a 952-byte stack workspace in XLogInsert() for each record, where before a static buffer was zeroed once. A small-record, high-insert workload pays this cost on every call, and nobody has measured it. In _mdfd_getseg(), each call also fills an 8 kB const zero buffer, and the stack frame grows to about 20 kB.
objections.argument: Patch 0005 adds the memset because the static variable used to be zero-initialized for free. Message #8 shows the memset is needed, since without it 16033 WAL records carry uninitialized padding bytes. No message measures the cost on the XLogInsert() path, which every WAL-writing user takes. Message #11 shows the _mdfd_getseg() and dsm_impl_mmap() const locals copy or clear 8 kB per call and suggests static const; v4 does not take that up.
objections.author_must_show: What does a pgbench or small-insert benchmark show for v4 0005 against master, and will the 8 kB zero buffers become static const?

critic.reasoning: Patch 0005 adds a memset of the workspace on every XLogInsert() call, and the thread shows no timing for it. Message #11's static const suggestion for the 8 kB zero buffers has no reply yet.

refuted.title: Reusing PGAlignedXLogBlock with weaker alignment breaks direct I/O silently
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension reads WAL segments with O_DIRECT into a PGAlignedXLogBlock. After 0001 plus 0003, it still compiles, but the buffer is only 8-byte aligned. pread then fails with EINVAL on ext4 and works on btrfs, so the failure appears only on some user systems.
refuted.argument: Message #8 shows this exact case: alignment drops from 4096 to 8, and O_DIRECT pread returns EINVAL on ext4 but not on btrfs. The out-of-tree users found there are WAL tools such as pg_tde and pg_wal_fp_extract, the kind of code that might add direct I/O later. 0001 alone turns the change into a compile error that names the replacement, which is safer. Message #7 shares the hesitation, but 0003 is still attached and has not been withdrawn.
refuted.author_must_show: Will 0003 be held back for at least one major release after 0001, so that out-of-tree users of the old name get a compile error first?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. Both describe the same O_DIRECT failure from 0003 and cite the same measurements in message #8.

refuted.title: Renaming PGAlignedXLogBlock breaks known extensions for naming consistency only
refuted.failure_scenario: pg_tde, pg_flashback, WAL-DIFF and other tools that declare PGAlignedXLogBlock fail to compile against the new major version. Their maintainers must add version conditionals. If 0003 later brings the name back with 8-byte alignment, any code that does direct I/O through the type starts failing with EINVAL on ext4 only.
refuted.argument: Message #8 lists at least seven out-of-tree users of the type, and the rename fixes no bug in core. Patch 0001's commit message leaves room for a MAXALIGNed PGAlignedXLogBlock later, so the project would be agreeing now to a second, silent change of meaning. The proposal does not offer a compatibility macro or a deprecation period, and it does not say how long the name must stay unused before it can come back.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is the naming gain worth breaking known extensions, and will the project promise never to reuse PGAlignedXLogBlock with weaker alignment?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2 for the rename and of standards-compat-1 for the later reuse of the name. It adds no separate scenario.

refuted.title: Rename of PGAlignedXLogBlock costs extension authors for naming consistency only
refuted.failure_scenario: Maintainers of pg_tde, pg_flashback, WAL-DIFF and the other repositories in message #8 rebuild against the new major version. Their builds fail on 'unknown type name PGAlignedXLogBlock', and each one adds version #ifdefs. If 0003 ships, those builds compile, but any direct-I/O user of the type fails with EINVAL on ext4 only.
refuted.argument: The rest of the series does not need the rename; message #7 gives naming symmetry with PGAlignedBlock and PGIOAlignedBlock as the only reason for it. Message #8 found at least seven out-of-tree projects that use the type, so the users bear the whole cost and get no new capability. The author treats 0003 as risky in message #7, so the choice is a compile break or a silent change in alignment. Keeping the old name, maybe with a comment, avoids both.
refuted.author_must_show: What does the rename to PGIOAlignedXLogBlock gain in core that is worth breaking the out-of-tree users listed in message #8?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2. The cost to the projects in message #8 and the option of keeping the old name are covered there.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: Patches 0004 and 0005 change how xloginsert.c builds the WAL record header; 0002 changes buffers in xlogreader.c.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: 0001 renames PGAlignedXLogBlock in c.h, 0003 reuses the name with weaker alignment, and the XLogReader struct in xlogreader.h changes.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: With 0003, PGAlignedXLogBlock means a different alignment in new and old branches, so back-patched code using the name behaves differently.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The pgindent workaround for alignas and the HEADER_SCRATCH_SIZE assertion are small new pieces to keep correct.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: 0005 zeroes a 952-byte local workspace in XLogInsert() for every WAL record.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Will 0003 be part of the commit, and if so, how many major releases will separate the rename in 0001 from the reuse of the name PGAlignedXLogBlock?
Why is renaming PGAlignedXLogBlock without a compatibility alias better than keeping the old name and choosing a new name for a MAXALIGNed block?
What does a small-record insert benchmark show for v4 with 0005 against master?
Will the zero buffers in _mdfd_getseg() and dsm_impl_mmap() become static const, as message #11 suggests?
Which call sites does 0002 convert, and how much stack does each one add?

committability.owner_note: The author is listed as Peter Eisentraut (petere), and Heikki Linnakangas reviewed the WAL insert part in message #2. The owner needs to know the WAL insert path and the direct I/O alignment rules.
committability.liability: The owner signs for zeroed padding in every WAL record header, for the stack use of the converted call sites, and for the meaning of PGAlignedXLogBlock in extension code across major releases.
committability.author_follow_up: The author answered the review comments in v3 and v4 and added the two patches that Heikki suggested. Message #11 has no reply yet.

priority.reason: This is internal refactoring that helps core developers and the multi-threading work, and it adds no user-visible surface apart from the type rename. The patches are small, but 0005 changes the WAL insert path, which needs a careful reader and a timing.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check that the memset in 0005 covers all padding, that the new assertion matches the HEADER_SCRATCH_SIZE calculation, or how much stack each converted call site uses. Only 3 of 11 messages were read directly.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Cache line alignment of PGXACT
precedents_retrieved.summary: Align each PGXACT entry in shared memory to a cache line, or to 16 bytes in a later version, so that entries do not share or straddle cache lines. The goal was to cut contention and raise pgbench -S throughput on machines with many cores.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Benchmarks showed read-only gains but regressions on read-write and mixed workloads, and the author judged the read-write loss about as large as the read-only gain. The author also found that padding PGPROC, or another unrelated alignment change, gave the same read-only effect, so it was unclear the patch itself was needed. The author returned the patch for more investigation.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It became clear that this patch causes regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: change SOFT_ERROR_OCCURRED to a static inline function
precedents_retrieved.summary: Change the SOFT_ERROR_OCCURRED macro to a static inline function that takes a Node *, so the compiler catches a wrong argument like the fcinfo->args bug fixed in timestamptz_date. Callers that pass an ErrorSaveContext * would get explicit casts to Node *.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut suggested changing the escontext field to Node * instead of adding casts. Nathan Bossart, who proposed the change, found that alternative too invasive for the gain: it needs more memory management and casts back to ErrorSaveContext * in many places. Typing the field as ErrorSaveContext * still needs casts to Node *, unless the function accepts void *, which defeats the type check. The thread ends there, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I started looking at this, but it seems to be a rather invasive change for
the level of gain.

precedents_retrieved.title: Get rid of the pre-C11 _Alignof define in zic.c
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the pre-C11 _Alignof define from zic.c and uses the C11 _Alignof instead, now that commit f5e0186f865c is in. It follows earlier use of _Noreturn in the same file.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the change adds a local difference from the upstream tzdb code in zic.c. He noted that a re-sync with recent tzdb is overdue and that changes like this one do not make it easier. The author withdrew the entry after that reply.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm not in favor of introducing random discrepancies from tzdb
upstream.

precedents_retrieved.title: Mingw: Fix import library extension, build actual static libraries
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes MinGW builds to give import libraries the .dll.a extension instead of .a, matching downstream workarounds in Fedora and Arch Linux packages. A second patch builds real static libraries next to the DLLs, which it describes as modeled on the AIX case in Makefile.shlib.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut found nothing in the MinGW documentation to support the .dll.a naming, since its examples match the current naming, and he asked the author for a source. Noah Misch pointed out that Postgres does not build static libraries on AIX, so the premise of the second patch was wrong. He also noted that static and import libraries would need different names. The visible thread shows no reply from the author before the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: All their examples match our existing naming.

precedents_retrieved.title: Report tranche ID and LWLock pointer in LWLock static tracepoints
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set adds the LWLock pointer and the numeric tranche ID to each LWLock static tracepoint, so traces can tell individual locks apart and compare them across processes. It also fixes misplaced tracepoints, adds a single tracepoint for all acquires and releases plus start markers for timing, and adds comments on LWLock tranches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Two parts were committed by Peter Eisentraut: the removal of the wrong lwlock__acquire tracepoint in LWLockWaitForVar, and the move of TRACE_POSTGRESQL_LWLOCK_RELEASE. In his last review he reported that patch 0002 did not build on macOS because uint64 was used in the probe definitions, and that the probe changes had no documentation. He also asked for a different argument order and whether both tranche name and tranche ID are needed. The visible messages show no new version after that review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
First, a problem:  0002 doesn't build on macOS, because uint64 has been
used in the probe definitions.

precedents_retrieved.title: Align verify_heapam.c error message offset with test expectations
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes three error messages in contrib/amcheck/verify_heapam.c to report the successor tuple's offset (nextoffnum) instead of the current line pointer (ctx.offnum). precedents_retrieved.title: psql BACKEND_PID variable
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a built-in psql variable BACKEND_PID, set from PQbackendPID() at connect time and unset when the connection is lost. The stated benefits were tab completion of :BACKEND_PID, listing in \set, and no need to rerun pg_backend_pid() after a reconnect.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane and Peter Eisentraut held that the variable duplicates pg_backend_pid() and the %p prompt escape without making a real task easier. Tom Lane noted that while a slow query runs, the variable cannot be read any more than the function can be run. He also said each new built-in variable adds clutter. Andrew Dunstan moved the entry from Ready for Committer to Rejected, citing these comments, and the author agreed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't buy Pavel's argument that adding Yet Another built-in variable
adds ease of use.  I think what it mostly adds is clutter.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fractions in GUC variables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets real-valued GUC settings be written as percentages, such as `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 20%`, in postgresql.conf and in SET. It also changes how four tagged settings are displayed, so SHOW returns them as percentages instead of fractions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The original reason for the TODO item went away when the bgwriter_*_percent settings were removed, and GUCs now use fractions consistently. Reviewers did not want to change the default display format, and accepting percentages only where they make sense (not for geqo_selection_bias or geqo_seed) would make the feature more complex. Bruce Momjian removed the TODO item.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Overall, I feel that this isn't really worth the trouble. We use fractions consistently now, so there isn't much room for confusion over what the current values mean.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict"
Reverted commit(s): Replace pg_restrict by standard restrict
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit f0f2c0c1aef95757c4e7f144d5577e2b0d814279.

The original problem that led to the use of pg_restrict was that MSVC
couldn't handle plain restrict, and defining it to something else
would conflict with its __declspec(restrict) that is used in system
header files.  In C11 mode, this is no longer a problem, as MSVC
handles plain restrict.  This led to the commit to replace pg_restrict
with restrict.  But this did not take C++ into account.  Standard C++
does not have restrict, so we defined it as something else (for
example, MSVC supports __restrict).  But this then again conflicts
with __declspec(restrict) in system header files.  So we have to
revert this attempt.  The comments are updated to clarify that the
reason for this is now C++ only.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent changes with durable_rename_excl()
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent changes with durable_rename_excl()
Reverted commit(s): Remove durable_rename_excl(); Replace existing durable_rename_excl() calls with durable_rename()
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits 2c902bb and ccfbd92.  Per buildfarm members
kestrel, rorqual and calliphoridae, the assertions checking that a TLI
history file should not exist when created by a WAL receiver have been
failing, and switching to durable_rename() over durable_rename_excl()
would cause the newest TLI history file to overwrite the existing one.
We need to think harder about such cases, so revert the new logic for
now.

Note that all the failures have been reported in the test
025_stuck_on_old_timeline.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. The only retrieved row, [P17], reverted a C11 change because standard C++ has no restrict; C++11 has alignas as a keyword, so that reason does not carry over to the alignas use in xlogreader.h. The thread points to no earlier discussion of this idea.
The other changes are internal refactoring. They add no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog or dump behaviour. Message #8 shows WAL contents are unchanged.

WAL content is unchanged: message #8 shows the memset in 0005 keeps the XLogRecord padding zeroed. The patch has no on-disk, catalog, or protocol change. The xlogreader.h struct change and the 0001 rename are normal API breaks in a major release.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It is internal refactoring of buffer allocation, and no user gains new rights, data or resources. The one possible exposure is uninitialized stack bytes in XLogRecord padding reaching the WAL, where replication and pg_waldump users can read them. Patch 0005 adds a memset for this, and message #8 measured zero non-zero padding bytes with it.
Two objections stand. Experienced committers wrote and reviewed this internal refactoring, so the maintenance-ownership risk is low.

Nothing in core or in an extension already does this job: the patch is internal refactoring that reuses existing mechanisms (C11 alignas, PGAlignedBlock, PGIOAlignedBlock), so no second way is added. The one existing idiom it could follow better is the static const zero buffer in pg_pwrite_zeros(), raised in message #11; that is an open review point, not a reason to reject.

The core refactoring (alignas locals, the HEADER_SCRATCH_SIZE assertion, removing statics in XLogRecordAssemble) is internal cleanup with no user-facing cost. Three reviewers support it and it helps the multi-threading work, so demand is not a valid objection to it.
